# One instant per batch

<!-- review-bot-scope:start -->
packages/store-*/src/**
packages/core/src/fenced-batch.ts
packages/core/src/sql-tree.ts
packages/core/src/statements/**
packages/conformance/src/invariants.ts
packages/conformance/test/clock-jitter.test.ts
scripts/clock-lint.py
scripts/batch-lint.py
scripts/lint-selftest.py
scripts/mutation-probe.py
<!-- review-bot-scope:end -->

Scope: all dialect source files under `packages/store-*/src/**` (including nested TypeScript and standalone SQL), the primitive that enforces the rule (`packages/core/src/fenced-batch.ts`), the statement trees it checks (`packages/core/src/sql-tree.ts` and the shared statements under `packages/core/src/statements/**`), and its executable twins — `packages/conformance/src/invariants.ts` (`one-batch-two-instants`), `packages/conformance/test/clock-jitter.test.ts`, `scripts/clock-lint.py`, `scripts/batch-lint.py`, `scripts/lint-selftest.py`, `scripts/mutation-probe.py`. This rule is only about WHEN a statement gets its instant. Whether a follow-on carries a fence at all, and whether that fence reaches every row it writes (the `OR`/`NOT`/selection shapes), belongs to the fence-provenance rule. Ambient JavaScript time in engine code — `Date.now`, `new Date`, timers — belongs to the determinism rule and `scripts/determinism-lint.sh`. Validation of client durations and absolute instants at the port (`durationToMs`, `requireEpochMs`) belongs to the numeric-boundary rule.

DESIGN.md §3.4 rule 3 says engine time is database time, and says exactly how far that reaches: the clock expression is stable WITHIN one statement — measured 4000/4000 identical for SQLite `unixepoch('subsec')`, including inside scalar subqueries — and is NOT stable across statements. Two statements of one local SQLite batch saw two different instants 94 times in 4000, about 2%, and far more over a network. Rule 8 draws the only safe line from that: only the guarded compare-and-set may read the clock, and every later statement derives its instants from the `fence_at_ms` that statement recorded. That column exists for this reason — without it the suspension marker would be a standing exemption to the ban.

This shipped repeatedly, in code that looked careful. `heartbeat` was two statements — the extend, then a `SELECT` computing `claim_expires_at_ms - <clock>` — so the remaining-lease number handed to a live worker was wrong by however far the two reads drifted; the fix collapsed it into one statement with `RETURNING claim_expires_at_ms - heartbeat_at_ms`, because a one-statement batch cannot have the problem at all. `claim`'s wait cleanup compared each wait's `timeout_at_ms` against a FRESH clock read, so waits falling due between two deliveries of the same claim were deleted by the delivery that had claimed nothing. `activate` compared a lease expiry taken at 1,060,000 against a cancel deadline taken at 1,060,001 and ran a claim-timeout sweep instead of a cancellation. And the checker built to prevent the class did not catch the class: `clock-lint` bans raw clock FUNCTIONS, so the sanctioned `NOW_MS` used in two statements sailed through (finding 16 — "a run due at one instant and its wait expiring at another lets a claim deliver an early timeout while leaving the wait registered"), and it was case-sensitive while SQL is not, so `UNIXEPOCH()` and `now()` passed too (finding 10). That round's automated machinery found 0 of 44 defects. Treat every twin named below as a net with known holes, not as coverage.

<!-- review-bot-synopsis:start -->
Flag a second database-clock read inside one batch — a raw wall-clock function, a re-spelled `NOW_MS`, or a `fake_now_ms` read in a package `clock-lint` does not walk (any casing) or in a new basename-exempt `time.ts`; `${NOW_MS}`/`${NOW}`/an alias/a clock-carrying fragment appearing in two statements of one `this.db.batch` or `FencedBatch` (including when hoisted into a constant, which `batch-lint` counts as zero); database time in any non-CAS statement; a hand-stamped follow-on whose `fence_at_ms` is not a stamped row's `fence_at_ms`; a first-write-wins conflict restamp that names a table or instant absent from the dialect-neutral preserved-instant enumeration; an engine instant computed in TypeScript and bound as `?`; CAS arms made mutually exclusive by a clock comparison; a non-statement-stable dialect clock (`SYSDATE()`, `clock_timestamp()`); a second clock definition beside `NOW_MS`; or a weakening of clock-lint/batch-lint/the FencedBatch clock guard/its mutation-probe entry/lint-selftest's spelling list/`one-batch-two-instants`/the clock-jitter test. Pass for any number of reads within ONE statement however aliased, mutually exclusive CAS arms that each read it, `sweep:scan`'s declared read-only pair, arithmetic on `fence_at_ms` via `fencedAt`, an instant copied from any column an earlier statement of the batch wrote, a follow-on's instant read off a different table the batch stamped, a stored protocol instant from an earlier transition used for its contract meaning, including the enumerated `events.emitted_at_ms` conflict restamp, `time.ts` and the `admin:*` doors, deliberate test clocks and lint-selftest fixtures, and a `requireEpochMs`-validated `atEpochMs` bound as `?`.
<!-- review-bot-synopsis:end -->

Report a failure when the changed code introduces or materially expands any of these:

- **Database time named where `clock-lint` cannot see it.** A raw wall-clock call or bare keyword in any casing (`unixepoch`, `strftime`, `julianday`, `datetime('now')`, `NOW()`, `SYSDATE()`, `CURDATE()`, `CURTIME()`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `LOCALTIME`, `UTC_TIMESTAMP`, `clock_timestamp()`, `statement_timestamp()`, `GETDATE()`), a re-spelled or re-indented copy of the `NOW_MS` expression, or a bare read of the `meta` / `fake_now_ms` override — appearing in `packages/core`, `packages/conformance/src`, `packages/driver`, `packages/sdk`, a SQL file outside a dialect's `packages/store-*/src` tree, or a dialect package whose sources do not sit there. Inside `packages/store-*/src`, `clock-lint` recursively audits both TypeScript templates and standalone `.sql` files and fails CI, so a finding there is noise, not a finding.
- **A second statement of one batch naming database time.** `${NOW_MS}`, `${NOW}`, whatever string a `FencedBatch` was constructed with as `now:`, a local alias holding it, or a fragment call carrying it (`cancelDue(task, NOW)`, `eligibleTask('t', NOW)`) — appearing in more than one element of a `this.db.batch([...])` array, or in more than one `cas`/`casMany`/`followOn`/`derived`/`tail` of one `FencedBatch`. Flag it especially when the SQL is hoisted into a module constant: `batch-lint` counts the literal text `${NOW_MS}` inside the call site, so `{ sql: MY_SQL_CONST }` reads as ZERO clock reads. `sweep:scan` is counted at 0 today for exactly that reason, and every `FencedBatch` is invisible to the counter entirely.
- **Database time in a non-CAS statement, even as the batch's only clock read.** A `followOn`, a `derived` `where`/`narrow`/`set`, a `tail` or an `openTail` that compares against or assigns from the clock. It has `fence_at_ms`. This is the shape behind the `activate` and claim-cleanup incidents above, and the one whose only guard — `!isCas && (sql.includes(NOW) || sql.includes(this.now))` — is an exact substring match that a re-spelling defeats.
- **A hand-stamped follow-on whose `fence_at_ms` is not a `fence_at_ms` of a row this batch stamped** — `fence_at_ms = ?`, a literal, or another column. `assertWritesStamp` only requires `/\bfence_at_ms\s*=/`, so `fence_stamp = $STAMP$, fence_at_ms = heartbeat_at_ms` constructs cleanly. No follow-on is hand-stamped text any more: spawn's `run`, `fail`'s and `sweep:claim-timeout`'s `successor`, and emit's `wake-runs` are shared statement trees, whose stamp and instant the tree rules read, and a bare instant in store text should come through `fencedAt(...)`. Generated `derived()` updates always take both values from their declared source fence.
- **A first-write-wins conflict restamp outside the dialect-neutral enumeration.** The only preserved fact instant is `(events, emitted_at_ms)`. An events conflict arm using `$NOW$`, another table or column, an expression, or a duplicate overriding assignment is a finding; another legitimate fact requires a contract entry and rejection tests.
- **An engine instant computed in TypeScript and bound as `?`** — a deadline, a lease expiry, a backoff target, a wake time. Rule 3: clients pass relative durations and the engine computes every absolute in SQL. The one exception is a client's own `atEpochMs`.
- **Two CAS arms of one batch whose mutual exclusivity rests on a clock comparison** — one guarded `deadline <= ${NOW}` and the other `deadline > ${NOW}`. Per-statement re-reads mean both can match or neither. Exclusivity must rest on state the clock cannot change between statements, as `sweep:lost-launch` does with `relaunch_count < CAP` versus `>= CAP`.
- **A new dialect, or a new `FencedBatch`, whose `now:` expression is not statement-stable in that dialect** — MySQL `SYSDATE()` (re-reads per call; `NOW(6)` is the statement's start time and is stable), Postgres `clock_timestamp()` (`statement_timestamp()` and `now()` are stable). §3.4 rule 3 names these individually; an unstable expression makes rule 8 unsatisfiable rather than merely risky.
- **A second definition of database time** — any new exported clock constant or inline clock expression alongside `NOW_MS`, including a cheaper or lower-precision one for a hot path. One expression, one home (`time.ts`), is what makes "read it once" a checkable claim.
- **Weakening a twin without instituting a replacement** — adding an entry to `MULTI_CLOCK`, or moving a batch into `SINGLE_WRITES`/`READS`, in `scripts/batch-lint.py`; adding a filename to `EXEMPT` or dropping an alternative from `CALLS` in `scripts/clock-lint.py`; deleting the clock guard in `fenced-batch.ts` or the `clock-ban-in-followon` entry in `scripts/mutation-probe.py`; removing a spelling from `lint-selftest.py`'s clock-lint reject list; loosening `one-batch-two-instants`; reducing `clock-jitter.test.ts` toward its no-jitter control.

Allowed cases (do NOT flag these):

- **The clock read many times in ONE statement, however spelled.** One statement is one instant, so all of these are correct: `claim`'s compare-and-set, `claimCas` in `packages/core/src/statements/claim-receipt.ts`, reads the clock many times: the `nowValue` node for `heartbeat_at_ms` and `fence_at_ms`, and `${NOW}` inside the store fragments it carries (`leaseExpiresAt`'s `${NOW} + ?`, `leaseFits`, and in the candidate subquery `r.available_at_ms <= ${NOW}` and `eligibleTask('t', NOW)`); `activateCas` and `deferLaunchCas` in the same file likewise; `spawn`'s `task` CAS four times; `heartbeat` and `expire-lease-now` twice each; `driver-heartbeat`'s INSERT twice (`VALUES (?, ?, ${NOW_MS}, ${NOW_MS} + ?)`); `admin:now`'s `SELECT ${NOW_MS} AS now_ms`.
- **A local alias or fragment holding the clock and spliced more than once inside ONE statement.** `reschedule`, `suspendRun`, and `deferLaunch` pass `prepareWake`'s wake expression as one fragment, and `parkAssignments` in `packages/core/src/statements/park.ts` places it twice in the same compare-and-set, once in the `state` CASE and once as `available_at_ms`; `cancelTransition` builds `const deadlineGuard = deadlineOnly ? \`${cancelDue('tasks', NOW)} AND \` : ''` and passes it inside the admission fragment of `cancelCas` (`packages/core/src/statements/cancel.ts`). Check where the splices LAND, not how many there are.
- **Several mutually exclusive CAS arms each reading the clock.** `sweep:lost-launch` has `reopen` and `cap`, both carrying `claim_expires_at_ms <= ${NOW}` in a shared `guard` string and both stamping. They are exclusive on `relaunch_count`, so at most one ever writes and only one instant is ever recorded.
- **`sweep:scan`'s two read-only discovery statements**, `SWEEP_SCAN_CANCELS_SQL` (whose `cancelDue('t', NOW_MS)` is a fragment carrying the clock at module scope) and `SWEEP_SCAN_EXPIRED_SQL`. Declared in `batch-lint`'s `MULTI_CLOCK` with its reason: read-only discovery, and every item is re-checked under its own fence, so an item sitting exactly on a deadline merely waits for the next tick.
- **Arithmetic on the fenced row's `fence_at_ms` in a follow-on.** `f.fence_at_ms + ${INFRA_BACKOFF_SECONDS} * 1000` (`sweep:claim-timeout`'s successor), `f.fence_at_ms + ?` (`fail`'s successor), `SELECT f.task_id, ?, f.queue, ?, f.run_id, f.attempt, f.fence_at_ms` (the suspend marker and `setCheckpoint`'s upsert), `timeout_at_ms <= ${fencedAt('runs', ...)}` (claim's `waits-timeout`), `${activated}` in `activate`'s `task-start`, and `available_at_ms = ${emitted}` in emit's `wake-runs`. This is what the column is for.
- **An instant copied from a row an earlier statement of the SAME batch wrote — including a non-provenance column of it.** `spawn`'s `run` takes `available_at_ms` from `f.enqueue_at_ms`, the deadline its task CAS just computed; `awaitEvent`'s `park` takes `available_at_ms` from `(SELECT f.timeout_at_ms FROM waits f WHERE … AND f.fence_stamp = …)`; `driver-heartbeat`'s second statement bounds its delete by `(SELECT d.last_beat_ms FROM drivers d WHERE …)`. Copying is the fix, not the bug.
- **A stamping follow-on taking `fence_at_ms` from a DIFFERENT fenced table this batch stamped.** Emit's `wake-runs`, the shared `wakeRunsUpdate`, selects runs but takes its gate and its `fence_at_ms` from the event row this batch recorded, deliberately: the event row gates the wake and provides its instant. The generated `wake-tasks` update then derives both values from the woken runs instead of hand-selecting a second provenance source.
- **A persisted instant from an EARLIER transition.** `activate`'s `task-start` computes `COALESCE(first_started_at_ms, ${activated})` and the max-duration deadline from it. Reading a stored timestamp written by a previous batch is not a second clock read.
- **The contract-enumerated events conflict restamp.** `emitEventCas` in `packages/core/src/statements/events.ts` assigns a fresh `fence_stamp` on conflict while copying `events.emitted_at_ms` into `fence_at_ms`; `FencedBatch` reads the conflict arm from the tree and refuses one that does not take the stamp or does not copy the table's preserved instant.
- **`packages/store-libsql/src/time.ts` itself, and the admin doors that own the override**: `admin:now`, `admin:set-fake-now`, `admin:clear-fake-now`.
- **Test code that deliberately moves the clock**: `JitteringExecutor` in `packages/conformance/test/clock-jitter.test.ts`, including its hand-written `UPDATE meta SET value = … WHERE key = 'fake_now_ms'`, and `openTestDb({ nowMs })`.
- **`scripts/lint-selftest.py`'s clock spellings.** Every raw wall-clock call appears there on purpose as a MUST-REJECT fixture; ADDING spellings strengthens the checker.
- **A user-supplied absolute bound as a parameter.** `reschedule` and `suspendRun`'s `atEpochMs` branch is a client instant validated by `requireEpochMs`, not a clock read. §3.4 rule 3 names `sleepUntil` as the one sanctioned user absolute.

A useful finding names four things. First, the batch label and the two statements that disagree — "`await-event`: `register` computes `${NOW} + ?` and `park` recomputes it" is actionable where "possible clock issue" is not. Second, the invariant: §3.4 rule 3 (database time, statement-stable only) or rule 8 (a follow-on may not read the clock; it has `fence_at_ms`). Third, the twin that should have caught it and the precise reason it could not — `clock-lint` bans functions, not the sanctioned expression, and only under `packages/store-*/src`, exempting any file named `time.ts`; `batch-lint` counts the literal `${NOW_MS}` only at readable-label `this.db.batch(` sites, so no `FencedBatch`, no alias, and no hoisted constant; `fenced-batch.ts` matches `this.now` as an exact substring and only outside a CAS; `one-batch-two-instants` sees only instants that reached two stamped rows sharing a seed, so a wrong instant RETURNED to a caller (the original `heartbeat` bug) or written into a non-provenance column of a single row leaves nothing for it to compare; `clock-jitter.test.ts` compares complete progress traces and every listed protocol table, but only for the operations and tables in its explicit inventories. Fourth, the fix shape: collapse into one statement, or derive through `fencedAt`, or a reference to the fenced row in a statement tree, from the `fence_at_ms` the CAS recorded. If no twin covers the shape, say so — this reviewer is a detection net of last resort, never a rung on the prevention ladder, so a defect it catches is a mechanism gap, and per CLAUDE.md the fix is not complete until that gap is closed at rung 1 or 2.
